label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
At four in the morning, someone makes toast.

I don’t know who started this. Nobody ever admits to being the person who put the first slices in. You become aware of the smell from the staff room, and then, if you can, you go and get some. Sometimes it’s cold by the time you eat it. It is still toast someone has made for you at four in the morning, which counts for quite a lot.

I did my last ever night shift on Saturday. Nine at night until half past seven on Sunday morning, in majors. After fourteen years, I’m moving onto a days-only rota.

I haven’t written here since spring. There are probably easier subjects with which to restart a neglected blog, but this is the one I keep coming back to. I thought I would feel straightforwardly pleased. Instead, I’ve been sad in a way that seems faintly ridiculous when I try to explain it. I have spent years wanting more sleep. Now I’m being given the opportunity, I appear to have objections.

There are sensible reasons for the change. My knees have developed opinions about my working life. My sleep has stopped recovering in the way I used to assume it always would. My GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is no longer something we can discuss as though it were an amusing administrative error.

At forty-two, I am apparently old enough to take this seriously.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing them for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. I would like that noted before anyone mistakes this for a theory about what happens to everyone after fourteen years. It is what has happened to me.

***

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. I remember very little of the actual shift. What I remember from that first winter is sitting in the car park at the Infirmary, crying because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose.

I had. I checked.

But I can still see the frost on the windscreen.

I don’t want to turn that younger version of myself into a story about how suffering made me a better doctor. She was tired and frightened, and she needed sleep. I wish I could tell her that she would learn more, become steadier, find people she trusted. I would also quite like to tell her to eat something and stop sitting in a freezing car.

There were other mornings like that, though not all with tears. Mornings when I took a worry home and carried it through the hours when I was supposed to be asleep. There were shifts I was proud of and shifts I was glad simply to have finished. Over fourteen years, those things get mixed together.

People sometimes assume that the attraction of emergency medicine at night is adrenaline. There is some of that, of course. But much of the work is less dramatic, and harder to describe.

It is explaining something again because the person in front of you is frightened and hasn’t taken it in. It is noticing that someone needs a blanket. It is managing not to make your exhaustion their problem.

Mostly, it is trying to stay kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

I haven’t always managed it as well as I wanted to. I’ve been impatient. I’ve heard my own voice come out sharper than it needed to be. I’ve also watched colleagues find patience when I would have sworn there was none left anywhere in the building, and tried to follow their example.

That is a large part of what nights gave me.

***

I’ve often thought the department is most itself at night.

There are fewer managers about, which is not an invitation to begin the usual argument. I’ve written enough about staffing and the NHS to know how easily I could spend the rest of this post there. This isn’t that post.

There is a particular honesty among people working through the small hours together. You learn who will notice you’re struggling before you say anything. You learn who can make you laugh when you really don’t want to. You get better, eventually, at asking for help.

There is kindness which doesn’t announce itself as kindness. Someone takes over for a few minutes. Someone checks whether you’ve had a drink. Someone puts bread in a toaster and denies all knowledge.

And there are moments with patients which stay, although they would barely register in an account of the medical work. An older man once held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands.

I won’t say more about him. He went home, and I was glad. But I have remembered what he said.

You can spend a great deal of a shift concentrating on what needs to happen next. Then someone says something like that, and for a moment you are paying attention differently.

I will miss those hours. I know people will still need kindness during the day. I know I will still have colleagues, and work, and reasons to feel useful. But I will miss being there at night, with that particular group of people, doing our best to get everyone through until morning.

***

It cost things too.

I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies because of nights. There was video, which I was grateful for, but it wasn’t the same as being there. My sister in Bangalore never once complained.

Her not complaining didn’t mean I hadn’t missed them. It meant she was being generous.

There are family events I can put a name to, and then there is the less memorable time: days off spent asleep, or too tired to do much, or waiting to feel normal again. Evenings when I was technically available but not very good company. Plans made with the qualification that I would have to see how I felt after nights.

For a long time I accepted that as part of the arrangement. Much of it was worth it. Some of it I would like back.

I’m relieved to be stopping. I’m relieved that I might sleep more reliably, that my body might have a chance to settle, that a day off might more often be a day I can use.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved.

Nobody has accused me of anything. My colleagues have been considerably more sensible about this than I have. Still, leaving nights feels different from changing a line on a rota. There are people I’m used to standing alongside, and now they’ll be there while I’m at home in bed.

I know the answer is not to keep doing something that is making me unwell. Knowing that hasn’t quite caught up with how I feel.

***

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road as the sun was coming up. I had the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up.

I realised I wouldn’t see that light from this side again: on my way home from a night shift, tired, finished, with the rest of the day beginning around me.

Of course I’ll see the sunrise again. Leicester is not withdrawing the service because I’ve changed rotas. But I’ve known that particular journey for fourteen years, and I hadn’t understood until then that I was attached to it.

From Monday, I’ll be on days. There will be plenty to learn about how to live with this new, much-wanted arrangement. For now, I think I can be grateful to have done nights and grateful to have finished them, even if the two feelings are making awkward company.

And tonight, or another night soon, someone will put bread in the staff-room toaster. Folasade will still beat people up the stairs. If they’re lucky, there will be a few minutes to sit down and eat.

I hope whoever makes the toast gets some while it’s hot.
